title: Sort Colors
description: Sort an array of 0s, 1s, and 2s in place in one pass, using the Dutch National Flag three-pointer technique.

blocks.text: Given an array nums containing only the values 0, 1, and 2, sort it in place so that all 0s come first, then all 1s, then all 2s, without using a library sort function.

blocks.caption: Three pointers partition the array into growing 0, 1, and 2 regions in a single pass.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums[] containing only 0, 1, 2"],["Output","The same array sorted in place: all 0s, then all 1s, then all 2s"],["Constraint","Must sort in place; a one-pass solution is possible"]]}

blocks.text: Sorting an array with only THREE distinct values is the classic Dutch National Flag problem: three pointers partition the array into a growing "0s" region on the left, a growing "2s" region on the right, and an unprocessed middle region that shrinks until it disappears.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This three-way partition generalizes the two-pointer partition idea (seen in Sort Array By Parity) from two groups to three.

Picture a row of red, white, and blue flags in random order. Three markers track the boundary of the red region (growing from the left), the boundary of the blue region (growing from the right), and the current flag being examined. Each flag is swapped into its correct region as it is examined.

blocks.caption: Three growing regions partition the array in a single sweep.

items: low marks the boundary up to which everything is a confirmed 0.
high marks the boundary from which everything is a confirmed 2.

mid scans forward: a 0 swaps with low and both advance; a 1 just advances mid; a 2 swaps with high, and high shrinks WITHOUT advancing mid (since the newly swapped-in value at mid has not been examined yet).

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The final array is [0,0,1,1,2,2], matching the expected output exactly.

A straightforward approach counts how many 0s, 1s, and 2s exist, then overwrites the array with that many 0s, followed by that many 1s, then that many 2s. This is correct and simple but requires two full passes over the array.

The Dutch National Flag technique achieves the same result in a SINGLE pass using three pointers, swapping each examined element directly into its correct region as the scan proceeds, without ever needing to count anything first.
Count occurrences of each of the three values in one pass, then overwrite the array in a second pass using those counts.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n)","One pass to count, one pass to overwrite"],["Space","O(1)","Just the fixed-size counts array"]]}

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: This is already O(n) time and O(1) space; the one-pass Dutch flag version below removes the need for a second full pass, useful when the array can only be scanned once (a true streaming constraint) or simply as a cleaner single-pass idiom.

Use three pointers: low and mid start at the beginning, high starts at the end. Scan with mid: a 0 swaps with low (both advance), a 1 just advances mid, and a 2 swaps with high (only high moves, since the newly swapped element at mid still needs to be examined). The scan ends when mid passes high.

items: nums[mid] == 2: swap(mid, high), high-- (mid stays, re-examining the new value there).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Passes"],"rows":[["Brute Force, count then overwrite","O(n)","O(1)","2"],["Optimized, Dutch flag three pointers","O(n)","O(1)","1"]]}

items: Sorting an array with exactly three distinct values is the Dutch National Flag problem, solvable in one pass with three pointers.
The 2-swap case is the subtle one: mid must NOT advance, since the newly placed value still needs to be classified.
This three-way partition generalizes the two-pointer partition pattern to any fixed small number of categories.

blocks.text: Sort Colors is solved with the Dutch National Flag three-pointer technique: low and high track the boundaries of the confirmed 0 and 2 regions, and mid scans through, swapping each value into place. Crucially, mid does not advance after a swap with high, since the newly placed value still needs to be examined, giving a single-pass O(n) time, O(1) space solution.
